title: Christmas at the Roosevelts'
subtitle: A President, a Closet, and a Smuggled Tree
intro: The president who protected 230 million acres had reservations about cutting an evergreen for one week indoors. His nine-year-old son had other ideas. Ten questions on Christmas in the Roosevelt house — including the last one.
heroAlt: President Roosevelt seated between his sons Archie and Quentin, 1904
heroCredit: President Roosevelt, Archie Roosevelt right side, Quentin Roosevelt left side, about 1904. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

badge.title: Christmas at the Roosevelts'

tiers.name: Waiting for Breakfast
tiers.line: The drawing room stays shut a while longer.

questions.prompt: What did Roosevelt think of Christmas trees while he was president?
options: He thought the whole business harmless enough
He disapproved of cutting evergreens
He insisted on the largest tree that would fit
He considered them a German import and said so
questions.explanation: A contemporary account put it plainly: in his trips to the woods he had seen the harm done by cutting down promising evergreens, so he did not believe very much in having a Christmas tree, and did not much want one in the house. Note what this is not — not a decree, not a ban on trees in the White House, and not, despite a century of retelling, a national ban on anything. A man with strong opinions about forests had one about his own parlour, and the household worked around it.
questions.imageAlt: President Roosevelt with Archie and Quentin
questions.credit: President Roosevelt, Archie Roosevelt right side, Quentin Roosevelt left side, about 1904. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Archie got a tree anyway. Where did he hide it?
options: In the stables
In the attic
In a big unused closet
Under his bed
questions.explanation: He smuggled a small evergreen into the house and set it up in a large closet nobody was using, then worked on it for days. Accounts differ on the accomplice — his father's own letter credits one of the White House carpenters, while a book published at the time gives the job to Quentin. Both may be right; Archie was persuasive.
questions.imageAlt: Archie and Quentin Roosevelt with their father
questions.credit: President Roosevelt, Archie Roosevelt right side, Quentin Roosevelt left side, about 1904. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What did Archie announce when he set out to do it?
options: “I’m going to fix up a tree”
“Father will never know”
“One tree cannot hurt a forest”
“We shall have Christmas properly”
questions.explanation: “I’m going to fix up a tree,” he said — and did. On Christmas morning, once the presents had been handed out, he and Quentin asked their father to come and look at the closet. “What is up now?” he asked. “Come and see!” they shouted. The door came open on a tree blazing with lights, and by every account he enjoyed it as much as anyone in the room.
questions.imageAlt: A room at Sagamore Hill with fireplace and mantel
questions.credit: Interior of Sagamore Hill with fireplace and bearskins. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Who else got presents off Archie's tree?
options: The White House ushers, by the president's order
Nobody — the tree was for the children only
The Secret Service men on duty that morning
Jack, Tom Quartz and Algonquin
questions.explanation: In his own account of the morning, Roosevelt lists a present each for Jack the dog, Tom Quartz the kitten and Algonquin the pony — animals Archie would no more think of neglecting, he wrote, than the president would think of neglecting Archie's brothers and sisters. Algonquin was the calico pony the Roosevelt boys once walked into the White House passenger lift to cheer up Archie when he was ill upstairs. It is a small line that tells you a great deal about that household.
questions.imageAlt: Quentin Roosevelt on a pony beside a White House policeman
questions.credit: Quentin Roosevelt on pony beside White House policeman. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: How were the presents kept secret in the weeks before Christmas?
options: The children were sent away until the day
A room was locked, and only Edith and one maid held a key
They arrived on Christmas Eve only
They were stored at the Treasury
questions.explanation: One room was turned into a storeroom for the season and kept locked, the key held by Mrs. Roosevelt and a single maid. Gifts arrived from all over the country — friends and strangers alike insisted on remembering the president — and on Christmas morning they were laid out on a large oval table by one of the tall windows.
questions.credit: The Parlor, Sagamore Hill. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: In his own childhood, where did the Roosevelt children hang their stockings?
options: In their parents' bedroom
In the nursery
At the foot of the stairs
On the drawing-room mantel
questions.explanation: In their parents' bedroom — and they used the biggest stockings they could borrow off a grown-up, which is a detail worth pausing on. On Christmas morning the children trooped in and ransacked them on their mother and father's bed. The larger presents waited downstairs behind a closed door until after breakfast, an almost unendurable wait.
questions.imageAlt: Tintype of the four Roosevelt children
questions.credit: The Roosevelt children. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What did he say about the Christmases of his own boyhood?
options: That they had been too solemn and churchy for his taste
That his own children's Christmases were far better
That he set out to reproduce them exactly
That he could scarcely remember any of them clearly
questions.explanation: He said he had never known anyone to have such attractive Christmases, and that in the next generation he tried to reproduce them exactly for his own children. The pattern he was copying is laid out in his Autobiography: stockings hung on Christmas Eve, opened before dawn while the children sat on their father and mother's bed, and the bigger presents arranged on a table for each child in the drawing room, the doors thrown open only after breakfast. For a man who changed nearly everything he touched, he left Christmas alone.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as a small boy
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, about two years old. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where did he spend Christmas 1918, his last?
options: In hospital in New York, too ill to travel
In Washington on political business
At the White House as a guest
At Sagamore Hill, home from hospital that morning
questions.explanation: He had been in hospital since November with rheumatism and inflammatory trouble, and Edith got him home to Oyster Bay in time for the day. Alice, Ethel, Archie and Grace were waiting at Sagamore Hill when she brought him in. Quentin, the boy from the closet story, had been shot down over France that July.
questions.imageAlt: Interior of Sagamore Hill with elephant tusks, antlers and a bison head
questions.credit: Interior of Sagamore Hill with elephant tusks, antlers and bison head. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What promise did he tell his sister he had kept?
options: To work up to the hilt until he was sixty
To finish his last book before the year's end
To visit every state in the Union
To never seek a third term
questions.explanation: On Christmas Eve, bandaged and bright-eyed in a hospital bathrobe, he told his sister Corinne: “I promised myself that I would work up to the hilt until I was sixty, and I have done it.” He had turned sixty eight weeks earlier. Republicans were already talking about nominating him again in 1920.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, seated portrait. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Leaving the hospital that Christmas morning, dizziness hit him in the lift. What did he tell his doctor?
options: “Not a word of this to the newspaper men outside”
“Say nothing of this to anyone in the corridor”
“I shall be perfectly well again by the first of the year”
“I am not sick and it will give the wrong impression”
questions.explanation: Dr. Richards reached out to steady him and he flinched: “Don’t do that, doctor. I am not sick and it will give the wrong impression.” Then he braced himself, walked the corridor unaided and got into his car. He died at Sagamore Hill twelve days later, on 6 January 1919.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt, seated portrait. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.
